chapter.title: Design YouTube
chapter.source: System Design Interview: An Insider's Guide by Alex Xu

overview: Design a YouTube-like video platform focused on two core flows: video upload and video streaming. The design uses CDN and blob storage, separates streaming from API traffic, transcodes uploads into multiple compatible formats/bitrates, uses a DAG-based processing pipeline, and adds optimizations for upload speed, parallelism, security, CDN cost, and fault tolerance.

capacity_estimation.takeaway: CDN bandwidth cost is a major architectural concern.

high_level_architecture.role: Uploads and watches videos on phone, browser, or TV.
Caches and streams video directly to viewers from nearby edge servers.
Handle everything except video streaming: signup, metadata, recommendations, upload URL generation, etc.

upload_components.role: Stores video metadata; sharded and replicated.
Caches video metadata and user objects.
Convert videos to suitable formats, codecs, resolutions, and bitrates.
Workers consume completion events and update metadata cache/DB.

actual_video_steps: Upload source video to original storage.
Transcoding servers fetch it and transcode it.
After transcoding, store encoded files in transcoded storage.
In parallel, enqueue a transcoding-completion event.
Completion handler updates metadata DB and cache.
API servers tell the client the video is ready.
upload_flow.metadata_flow: While the file uploads, the client separately sends metadata such as file name, size, and format through API servers to Metadata Cache and Metadata DB.

download_vs_streaming.download: Whole video is copied to the device.
download_vs_streaming.streaming: Client receives a little data at a time so playback can begin immediately.

streaming.important_point: Choose a streaming protocol compatible with required encodings and playback players.
streaming.delivery: Video is streamed directly from the CDN edge server nearest the viewer.

why_needed: Devices and browsers support different formats.
Higher bandwidth users can receive higher-quality versions.
Lower bandwidth users can receive lower-resolution versions.
Network conditions change, so quality should be switchable.
transcoding.bitrate: Rate at which bits are processed over time; higher bitrate generally means higher quality and higher resource/network requirements.

container.definition: Wrapper containing video, audio, and metadata.

dag_model.purpose: Represent video-processing tasks as stages that may run sequentially or in parallel.
why: Different creators may require different processing pipelines.
DAG abstraction supports flexibility and parallelism.

preprocessor: Perform server-side GOP splitting for old clients that cannot do it.
Generate a DAG from configuration files.
Cache/persist GOPs and metadata in temporary storage for retries.
transcoding_architecture.dag_scheduler: Split the DAG into stages and place tasks into the resource manager's task queue.

resource_manager.worker_queue: Priority queue containing worker utilization info.

transcoding_architecture.task_workers: Execute DAG-defined tasks; different workers may specialize in different tasks.

temporary_storage.metadata: Memory/cache because it is small and frequently accessed.
temporary_storage.cleanup: Free temporary data after video processing finishes.

speed.name: Chunked/resumable upload
speed.details: Split by GOP alignment; upload chunks instead of the whole file so failed uploads can resume.

speed.name: Upload centers close to users
speed.details: Use geographically distributed upload centers; the chapter proposes CDN infrastructure for this.

speed.name: Parallelism with message queues
speed.details: Insert queues between modules so downstream workers can consume jobs independently rather than blocking on upstream stages.

security.name: Pre-signed upload URL
flow: Client requests pre-signed URL from API server.
Client uploads directly using the signed URL.

security.name: Video protection
options: DRM: Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady

cdn_cost_optimization.observation: Video popularity follows a long-tail distribution: a few videos are very popular, many receive few or no views.
strategies: Serve only the most popular videos from CDN; serve less popular videos from high-capacity storage video servers.
For less popular content, keep fewer encoded versions; short videos may be encoded on demand.
Do not distribute region-specific popular videos to regions where they are not popular.
At very large scale, consider building a CDN and partnering with ISPs.

error_handling.recoverable: Retry several times; if it continues failing, return an error.
error_handling.non_recoverable: Stop associated tasks and return an error, e.g. malformed video.

playbook.split_video_error: If old client cannot split, upload whole video and split server-side.
playbook.api_server_down: Route to another stateless API server.
playbook.metadata_cache_down: Use replicated cache node and replace failed node.
playbook.metadata_db_slave_down: Use another slave for reads and replace failed server.

wrap_up.api_scaling: API servers are stateless, so scale horizontally.

differences: Higher latency requirements may require different streaming protocols.
Less parallelism is needed because small chunks are processed in real time.
Error handling must be faster; slow recovery is unacceptable.

wrap_up.video_takedowns: Violating videos can be detected during upload or via user flagging and then removed.

short_answer_questions.question: Why does the design use CDN and blob storage instead of building them?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: They are complex and costly to build at scale, and the interview should focus on choosing appropriate infrastructure rather than reimplementing every subsystem.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the upload pipeline.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Original storage -> transcoding -> transcoded storage/CDN plus completion queue -> completion handler -> metadata update -> client marked ready.

short_answer_questions.question: Why is transcoding required?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Raw video is huge; devices support different formats; users have different bandwidth; network conditions change, so multiple quality/format variants are necessary.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain container vs codec.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Container packages video/audio/metadata, such as .mp4. Codec compresses/decompresses video, such as H.264 or VP9.

short_answer_questions.question: Why use a DAG?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It lets different processing tasks and dependencies be configured while supporting parallel execution.

short_answer_questions.question: Explain the resource manager.
short_answer_questions.model_answer: It manages a priority task queue, worker-utilization queue, running queue, and a scheduler that matches high-priority tasks to suitable workers.

short_answer_questions.question: How are uploads sped up?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Split videos into GOP chunks for resumable upload and use upload centers geographically close to users.

short_answer_questions.question: How does the chapter reduce CDN cost?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Exploit long-tail popularity: CDN for popular content, fewer/on-demand encodings for unpopular content, regional placement, and potentially owned CDN/ISP partnerships.

short_answer_questions.question: How is failure handled?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Retry recoverable work, stop malformed/non-recoverable work, and use replicas, failover, rescheduling, and stateless rerouting for infrastructure failures.

short_answer_questions.question: What changes for live streaming?
short_answer_questions.model_answer: Latency requirements are stricter, a different streaming protocol may be needed, parallelism requirements are lower, and slow error recovery is unacceptable.
